title: Jonah Believes (Every Time)

pages.text:
Saturday number seven started with the same roar, but I didn't wait for it to finish. By 11:00, I was out of bed, shoes laced, and heading for the door. I knew Jonah would be in his room, laminating something. I knocked once.

He opened the door wearing his helmet. It was indoors, but he always wore it indoors anyway. He stared at me with the specific surprise of a boy who has just been told his dog can do algebra.

"Max?"

"Jonah."

"Did you... did you sleep?"

"I have," I said. "Listen. The day is repeating. The clock, the house, everything. It's the same Saturday."

He blinked. His eyebrows went up, then down, then up again. He didn't laugh. He just looked at me with a kindness that felt like a wet towel on a sunburn.

"Okay," he said softly. "Do you want a granola bar? Maybe it's the sugar."

I stood in the doorway, holding the air, and realized that knowing exactly what he was going to say was worse than him not believing me at all. It was like watching a movie in the theater where you know every line before the actor says it. You can't stop them. You can't change the script. You just have to stand there and listen to someone you trust gently try to fix a problem that isn't broken.
pages.image: Max in a red hoodie stands in a doorway looking tired while Jonah, an 11-year-old boy in a bike helmet, holds out a granola bar with a worried, kind expression; morning light, bedroom background.

pages.text:
I needed proof. I wanted to show him something that wasn't in the script, something only we knew. So I waited. I watched him write "4:10" in his notebook, then I watched him look at me when I predicted Mrs. Abernathy’s hot dish line. He was polite, and he was skeptical, and he was being a good friend, which is the worst thing a person can do when you are telling them the world is a loop.

Then I played my ace. I took a breath.

"Jonah," I said. "You cried at the end of that dog movie. The one with the golden retriever and the train station. You cried in the back row, and you didn't wipe your face, you just stared at the screen until the credits rolled."

His face went white, then pink, then a shade of red I didn't have a name for. He looked at the floor, then at me, then at the floor again, while his hands shook slightly.

"Okay," he whispered. "I believe you."

It wasn't a question, and it wasn't a debate. It was a surrender. He believed me because I knew a secret that no one else in the world knew. And I realized, standing there in the hallway, that I was the only person in the universe who was allowed to know. That was a heavy, silent thing to hold.
pages.image: Jonah in a bike helmet stands in a hallway looking shocked and pale, hands slightly raised; Max in a red hoodie stands nearby, serious and quiet; indoor lighting, tense mood.

pages.text:
Jonah is the best person to have a time loop with. He doesn't panic or cry; he gets a laminator. By 2:00, we had a chart, and by 3:00, we had hypotheses involving wormholes, the clock, and cheese. I am not joking about the cheese. He genuinely believed the block in the fridge was causing temporal displacement, and I let him think that because it was funnier than explaining quantum physics to an eleven-year-old in a bike helmet.

We spent the afternoon chasing the sprinkler on purpose. We ran to the Grady house and stood directly in the path of the water at 4:10, getting completely soaked until our shoes squelched like wet socks. We dried off on the porch, and then we ate ice cream at Scoops because we knew exactly when the day would end. It was the best afternoon I had in the whole month. For once, the world felt like a video game I had finally learned how to play, with a cheat code hidden in the code.

At 9:30, his mom leaned out of the kitchen window and called him in for the night, and I watched his face change as the belief, the laughter, and our shared secret all began to wash away like rain off a windshield. He said goodbye, turned around, and walked away into the night. I was left standing on the porch, wet and happy and completely alone.
pages.image: Max and Jonah, both in casual clothes and bike helmets, stand on a porch covered in water droplets, laughing; a sprinkler sprays water in the background; warm, joyful afternoon light.

pages.text:
I walked home slowly, watching the streetlights flicker on one by one, each one buzzing like a bee trapped in a jar. The house was dark, and I knew exactly what would happen at 6:47. Gus would roar, then the slipper would vanish, and the toast would burn before the smoke alarm even finished its first beep. Jonah would be in his room, wearing his helmet and holding a granola bar, asking if I had slept. This Jonah, the one who had believed me and run in the rain with me, would be gone. Replaced by a copy. A new version of the same boy.

I thought about it for a long time. I sat on the stairs, looking at my hands, realizing I had to prove myself again. I had to say the dog movie line. I had to watch his face go white and pink. I had to be the only one who remembered the rain. It felt like trying to teach a new kid the secret punch in a video game, knowing he would forget it by the next save point. It was like writing a letter and knowing it would be deleted before it arrived. But I didn't care. Not yet. I was tired and hungry, ready to sleep.
pages.image: Max in a red hoodie sits alone on a staircase in a dark hallway, looking thoughtful and lonely; dim lighting, shadows, quiet mood.

pages.text:
Saturday number eight began with the roar, followed by the slipper theft and the burnt toast, a routine I could recite like a multiplication table. At 11:00 sharp, I knocked on Jonah’s door. He opened it, helmet on, granola bar in hand.

"Did you sleep?"

I told him. I waited for the fear, the confusion, the quiet belief.

"Okay. I believe you," he said.

He used the exact same tone. The same timing. Every single detail was identical.

I laughed. It escaped before I could stop it, a loud, ugly sound that felt like popping a zipper in the wrong direction. I wiped my eyes and stared at the ceiling, then back at Jonah, who looked confused but kind.

"It's the same Jonah every time," I said to the air, to the missing clock, to the whole empty world. "And I get to be the only one who's different."

I grabbed the granola bar and ate it. It tasted like cardboard and honey, which was good. If nothing lasts, if the day is just a copy of a copy, then I was going to have the best time of my life. I would decide what mattered. Or I would decide that nothing did. But it would be my choice, not the clock's.
pages.image: Max in a red hoodie stands in a doorway eating a granola bar, smiling sadly and fiercely; Jonah in a bike helmet looks on with concern; bright, clear morning light.
